strengths: Addresses an important problem: stable, low-variance pathwise policy gradients in a fully on-policy setting without large replay buffers.
Combines maximum-entropy exploration, joint entropy/KL tuning, TD(lambda)-style value targets, and recent architecture/value-learning components into a complete on-policy actor-critic algorithm.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 23 DMC and 8 ManiSkill tasks with PPO, SAC, and FastTD3 baselines, multiple seeds, aggregate metrics, sample-efficiency curves, wall-clock comparisons, and memory comparisons.

Ablations isolate the effects of HL-Gauss categorical critic loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction, and KL regularization, showing especially clear benefits from HL-Gauss and KL constraints.

Strong practical results: competitive with FastTD3 at much lower memory, often wall-clock competitive with PPO, and reported robustness across many tasks with a largely shared hyperparameter configuration.
The paper promises JAX and PyTorch implementations, which supports reproducibility if the code and missing appendices are provided.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: the method combines existing ideas -- reparameterized/pathwise policy gradients, TD(lambda), maximum-entropy RL, KL-constrained updates, automatic temperature tuning, and modern critic architecture tricks -- and does not sufficiently position itself against prior stochastic value-gradient/on-policy value-gradient methods.

Several technical equations and algorithmic statements are inconsistent: Eq. 19/Algorithm 1 use the entropy target in the KL multiplier update, Algorithm 1 computes reverse KL while the text argues for forward KL, and the target/policy losses mix alpha and exp(alpha) conventions.

The value-target formulation is unclear and inconsistent: Eq. 14 uses MSE while Algorithm 1 uses cross-entropy HL-Gauss, Eqs. 12-13 have confusing indexing/normalization, and Eq. 21's clipped objective is malformed.

The pathwise gradient for stochastic policies is not properly derived: Eq. 9 omits the reparameterization/noise expectation, and the algorithm does not specify how gradients backpropagate through sampled actions.
Theoretical support for the central claim is weak: there is no convergence, bias-variance, or constrained-optimization analysis; joint entropy/KL Lagrangian tuning is mainly heuristic.

Evaluation has weaknesses: REPPO is run with more seeds than baselines, normalization is by the best return across algorithms, ablations are only on DMC, and comparisons to prior on-policy KL/MPO-style or value-gradient methods are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the stated code URL is missing in the manuscript, Appendix A on HL-Gauss appears absent, and per-environment tuning of discount factors/HL-Gauss ranges weakens the single-hyperparameter-set claim.
Scope is limited to GPU-parallelized state-based benchmarks; the claimed memory advantage for complex observations such as images is not empirically tested.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reducing variance and instability of on-policy policy gradient methods via pathwise gradients and learned value functions.

Integrates several recent and classical techniques into a coherent algorithm: TD(λ) value targets, maximum entropy exploration, KL-constrained policy updates, categorical Q-learning with HL-Gauss, layer normalization, and auxiliary self-prediction.
Empirical evaluation is broad: 23 tasks from Mujoco Playground DMC and 8 ManiSkill environments, with multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and ablation studies.

Reports strong empirical results: REPPO outperforms tuned PPO on both benchmarks, is competitive with FastTD3 under large-buffer settings, and shows lower memory footprint and good wall-clock performance in JAX.
Provides code, hyperparameters, and architecture details, which supports reproducibility.
Ablations identify KL regularization and HL-Gauss categorical critic as important design components, offering practical insights.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: on-policy pathwise policy gradients with learned value functions have been explored before, e.g., Stochastic Value Gradients (Heess et al., 2015) and related on-policy deterministic actor-critic methods. The paper neither compares to nor adequately positions against these works, and its claim of 'unlocking' on-policy pathwise gradients is overclaimed.

Technical inconsistencies undermine soundness: Eq. (19) updates the KL multiplier β using the entropy constraint instead of KL divergence; Eq. (20) uses actions sampled from the behavior policy and a KL term of the wrong sign (effectively reverse KL), contradicting Algorithm 1 and the stated use of forward KL. The TD(λ) equations are also non-standard and inconsistent with the pseudocode.

The algorithm pseudocode omits the reparameterization trick, which is essential for pathwise gradients through stochastic policies. Without it, the gradient through sampled actions is not correctly computed, making the core method unclear and potentially invalid as presented.

Evaluation concerns: normalizing returns by the maximum achieved by any algorithm may inflate REPPO's relative performance; unequal seed counts (10 for REPPO vs. 4 for PPO and 5 for FastTD3) can bias confidence intervals; and no comparison is made to key baselines such as SVG, MPO, or other on-policy pathwise/DPG variants.

Claims about stability and removal of target networks/double-Q are not theoretically justified, and no analysis of Q-value accuracy, bias, or overestimation is provided to support the assertion that a single on-policy critic suffices.

Memory comparison is not apples-to-apples: REPPO uses a 131,072-transition batch (1024 envs × 128 steps) while the constrained FastTD3 buffer is 32,768 transitions, so the 'similar memory' claim is misleading.
Reproducibility gaps: the manuscript states code is available at an address but no URL is provided; framework-specific wall-clock differences are acknowledged but not rigorously controlled.

Writing and clarity are below the standard for a top-tier conference: numerous typos, undefined notation, inconsistent equations, and formatting errors make the paper difficult to follow and reduce confidence in the technical details.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important problem: using pathwise policy gradients in a fully on-policy setting without requiring large replay buffers, by learning a sufficiently accurate Q-function from on-policy data.

Provides a coherent algorithmic recipe (REPPO) that combines maximum-entropy TD(λ) targets, KL-constrained policy updates with joint entropy/KL tuning, categorical Q-learning via HL-Gauss, layer normalization, and auxiliary self-prediction.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: 23 DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, multiple seeds, aggregate metrics with confidence intervals, sample-efficiency curves, wall-clock comparisons, memory comparisons, and design ablations.

Strong reported results: REPPO outperforms tuned PPO and SAC on aggregate metrics, is competitive with FastTD3 despite being on-policy and using orders-of-magnitude less memory, and shows better policy-improvement reliability.
Reproducibility is supported by sample implementations in both JAX and PyTorch, detailed hyperparameters, and supplementary implementation notes.
weaknesses: Several technical/notation inconsistencies may hinder reproducibility: the finite-horizon λ-return normalization in Eq. (13) appears incorrect; the critic loss in Eq. (14) is MSE while the algorithm and Section 3.2.1 use categorical cross-entropy; Eq. (16) constrains KL(πθ||πθ′) while Eq. (20) estimates KL(πθ′||πθ) from old-policy samples; and Eq. (19) updates β using H_target instead of KL_target.

The theoretical grounding is limited: there is no formal analysis of the bias/variance tradeoff, convergence, or conditions under which an on-policy learned Q-function is accurate enough for pathwise policy gradients, and the constrained optimization relaxation is mostly heuristic.

The hyperparameter-robustness claim is only partially supported: the method automatically tunes γ, vmin, and vmax per environment, and the main experiments use a single core hyperparameter setting with limited sensitivity analysis beyond selected ablations.

Ablations are informative but mostly restricted to DMC and two batch sizes; the auxiliary self-prediction loss has inconsistent effects across tasks, and layer normalization is found not very critical, so the claimed architectural importance is task-dependent.

Baseline coverage is uneven: ManiSkill compares only against PPO, not SAC or FastTD3, and wall-clock comparisons are limited to PPO on DMC. Some environments show PPO winning, and exploration/premature-convergence failures are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: enabling pathwise policy gradients in fully on-policy RL without replay buffers, which could reduce variance and memory footprint compared to score-based on-policy methods.

Broad empirical evaluation across 23 DMC and 8 ManiSkill tasks, with aggregate metrics and 20 seeds for the main method, showing strong final performance, sample efficiency, and reliability relative to PPO and other baselines.

Includes informative ablations isolating several components (KL regularization, HL-Gauss critic loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction), finding that KL regularization and categorical value learning are particularly important.
Provides practical comparisons to off-policy FastTD3 under different replay-buffer budgets, supporting the claimed memory advantage of on-policy training.
Likely reproducible: the paper specifies architectures, optimizer, key hyperparameters, and states that JAX and PyTorch implementations are available.
The proposed method is simple to implement relative to many trust-region/mirror-descent alternatives and appears robust across continuous and discrete action settings.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the core ingredients—pathwise gradients via a learned Q function, entropy regularization, KL-constrained policy updates, HL-Gauss value learning, layer normalization, and auxiliary self-prediction—are all existing techniques. The main contribution is an empirical demonstration that these can be combined effectively in an on-policy setting.

Theoretical grounding is weak. The constrained policy objective is relaxed into a heuristic clipped loss (Eq. 15) that switches objectives based on whether the KL constraint is violated; this is not a principled Lagrangian solution and is not theoretically justified.

The pathwise gradient expression in Eq. 5 is written for deterministic policies; for stochastic reparameterized policies the gradient should include the noise variable and its dependence on the policy parameters. The exposition is imprecise for the stochastic policies actually used.

The KL and entropy multiplier updates are heuristic root-finding rules without convergence guarantees. The paper claims hyperparameter robustness, but the method still relies on automatic per-environment tuning of discount factors and HL-Gauss ranges, and the entropy target scales linearly with action dimension.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Several PPO/SAC numbers are taken from prior work, FastTD3 is run with fewer seeds, and wall-clock comparisons are limited to PPO in JAX because other baselines lack comparable JIT-compilable implementations. This weakens claims of superior wall-clock efficiency across the board.

The auxiliary self-predictive loss is reported to be inconsistent across environments and sometimes harmful, yet it is included as a default component. This undermines the claim of a single robust default configuration and complicates practical adoption.

Ablations are primarily on DMC; the ManiSkill evaluation does not isolate the contribution of each architectural component. The discrete-action variant is only briefly explored in an appendix and underperforms PQN, which limits the generality claim.

The manuscript overstates some claims relative to the evidence: e.g., “superior sample efficiency, wall-clock time, memory footprint, and hyperparameter robustness” is not uniformly supported by apples-to-apples experiments, and no theoretical or rigorous empirical analysis of the bias introduced by the learned Q surrogate is provided.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well motivated, with an intuitive explanation of score-based vs. pathwise gradient estimators.
The empirical study is broad, covering 23 DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, with 20 seeds for REPPO and PPO, ablations, memory measurements, and reliability metrics.
The proposed method is simple and practical, and the authors provide both JAX and PyTorch implementations, which supports reproducibility.
The results show strong performance against PPO and competitive performance against off-policy baselines such as FastTD3, while avoiding large replay buffers.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: REPPO largely combines existing ideas—on-policy actor-critic learning, pathwise/deterministic policy gradients, maximum-entropy RL, KL-constrained updates, adaptive temperatures, HL-Gauss critics, layer normalization, and auxiliary self-prediction—without a fundamentally new insight. The main contribution is an engineering integration, and the paper does not sufficiently isolate which novel component drives the gains.

Technical inconsistencies in the method description: the TD-lambda target in Eq. (7)-(8) includes entropy terms for the current action and uses a different indexing convention than the soft Q-learning target used in Algorithm 1, which instead subtracts entropy for the next action. The paper also describes D_KL as KL(pi_theta || pi_theta') in Algorithm 1 but uses log(pi_theta'/pi_theta) with behavior-policy samples in Eq. (15), which estimates the reverse KL and is not clearly justified.

The central claim that pathwise policy gradients are effective in fully on-policy learning is only demonstrated empirically, without theoretical conditions or analysis of when the learned Q surrogate is accurate enough. Since the estimator is biased and the Q function is trained on behavior-policy actions while the actor samples current-policy actions, there is no guarantee that the KL constraint prevents harmful out-of-distribution actions.

Evaluation concerns: baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. PPO is compared at different training budgets in some plots, FastTD3 uses only 5 seeds, and several baselines are taken from prior papers rather than retuned under the same protocol. The paper does not include important on-policy KL/entropy-constrained baselines such as TRPO, MPO, or V-MPO.

Claims about superior wall-clock time, memory footprint, and hyperparameter robustness are stronger than the evidence. Wall-clock comparisons are only against JAX PPO and not against other baselines; memory advantages are shown mainly against off-policy methods, while on-policy PPO already has a similar memory profile; hyperparameter robustness is asserted but not systematically quantified across the claimed 30+ tasks.

Ablations show that KL regularization and HL-Gauss are important, but they do not clearly establish that the pathwise gradient itself is the main source of improvement over a well-tuned score-based on-policy method. The score-based Q variant is a strawman relative to modern PPO-style methods, and the GAE variant performs worse than vanilla PPO, suggesting the proposed framework may be sensitive to the estimator/objective combination.

Some implementation and reproducibility details are unclear, including the exact treatment of the entropy term in the pathwise gradient, the KL estimator used in practice, and the stability of the auxiliary loss across environments. The paper also omits code availability in the submitted PDF snippet, despite mentioning it.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the high variance and instability of score-based on-policy policy gradients, and demonstrates that pathwise policy gradients can be effective in a fully on-policy setting without replay buffers.

Introduces REPPO, a clear and well-motivated algorithm that combines maximum-entropy exploration, KL-constrained policy updates, and on-policy multi-step TD-lambda value learning; the removal of importance sampling and replay buffers is practically valuable.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation across 23 Mujoco Playground DMC tasks, 8 ManiSkill tasks, and an Atari-10 discrete-action suite, with aggregate metrics, confidence intervals, ablations, reliability analysis, memory comparison, and wall-clock discussion.

Reports strong empirical results: REPPO outperforms PPO and SAC on major benchmarks, is competitive with FastTD3 while using orders-of-magnitude less memory, and shows stable learning across more than 30 tasks with a largely shared hyperparameter set.

Reproducibility is strong: implementations are provided in JAX and PyTorch, hyperparameters and architecture details are documented, and ablations isolate the roles of KL regularization, HL-Gauss loss, normalization, and auxiliary tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily algorithmic integration rather than fundamental theoretical advance: pathwise gradients, entropy regularization, KL constraints, HL-Gauss, layer normalization, and auxiliary tasks are all existing components, and the paper does not provide convergence or performance guarantees for the combined on-policy scheme.

The core pathwise update relies on an accurate action-conditioned Q-function, but Q is trained on behavior-policy data while policy updates evaluate Q on newly sampled actions from the updated policy. The KL constraint mitigates but does not formally resolve the resulting out-of-distribution value-estimation issue.

Some comparison caveats remain: wall-clock comparisons focus on JAX PPO while other baselines lack directly comparable implementations; several baselines are taken from prior work under potentially different horizons/hyperparameters; FastTD3 is run with only 5 seeds; and ManiSkill PPO horizon differences require care in interpretation.

Hyperparameter-robustness claims are somewhat overstated: some hyperparameters such as gamma and HL-Gauss value ranges are auto-tuned per environment, the auxiliary task has inconsistent effects across tasks, and the discrete variant is slightly behind PQN.

The memory-footprint advantage is largely inherent to on-policy versus off-policy learning rather than unique to REPPO, and the paper does not compare against other on-policy pathwise or trust-region variants that might provide a more direct novelty baseline.
